name: Agent Database Access and Permissions
title: Agent Database Access and Permissions
answer: When an AI agent queries a database on behalf of a user, it should see only what that user may see. Row level security, scoped credentials, read only roles and audit logging are the controls that keep an agent from becoming a way around existing permissions. The topic covers how an agent's identity is established, how that identity is mapped to database roles and policies, and how the same rules apply whether the query comes from a person, a script or a model. It also covers the failure modes, such as a shared service account that grants more access than any single user would hold.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the database and warehouse permission systems that already exist, including roles, grants, views, row level security policies and connection pooling. Agents usually reach these systems through a gateway, a driver or a protocol server, and this site tracks 2451 active Model Context Protocol servers, 263 of them for SQL databases and warehouses. Credentials come from a secret manager or a token service rather than being pasted into a prompt or a configuration file. Every page on this site is built from a PostgreSQL database, so the same permission model applies to the pages that describe it.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start by mapping the agent to a database identity, often a dedicated role with read only grants and a short lived credential. Each request carries the user context, usually through a session variable or a signed token, so row level security policies can filter rows to what that user may see. Queries are parameterized, checked against an allowlist of tables and statements, and logged before and after execution. Teams test the setup with a permission matrix that compares what the agent returns for each user against what the user can retrieve directly. Generated SQL is reviewed or constrained, because a model that can write arbitrary joins can also write a query that reveals more than intended.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Audit logging is the record of what the agent asked, which user it acted for, what rows came back and when. That record is itself sensitive, so access to logs, retention periods and redaction rules need the same care as the data they describe. Provenance matters when an answer is reused, because a result produced under one user's permissions should not be passed to another user without rechecking. Access reviews, least privilege and clear ownership of agent credentials are the usual controls, and data protection rules apply to agent mediated queries just as they do to direct ones.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Agent access is moving toward delegated authorization, where the agent carries a token that names the user and the scope rather than a standing database password. Work on agent identity and on protocol servers continues, and the 263 SQL servers tracked here are one sign of how quickly the connection layer is filling in. Expect more fine grained policies, shorter credential lifetimes and better tooling for reviewing what an agent did. The hard part is likely to remain organizational, since permissions that were never cleaned up for people will not clean themselves up for agents.
